notes:
Atkin page 7, with typed 6 cancelled and handwritten 7 added, continues the b(n) examples, then gives the normalized multiplicative conjecture (3.8), the unramified relation (3.9), and its ramified version (3.10). The author says (3.9) was tested for alpha≤8, p≤97 and pn≤1000 and was recently proved in general. Those computational and proof claims are reported, not reproduced. The typescript has conjecutre with a transposition cue and comgruence with m cancelled and n supplied. The handwritten insertion from (3.2) attaches after show. The formula (3.11) continues onto the next sheet, where P is specified.

S047-EXPONENT: For p prime to 13, Fermat’s relation p^12=1 in the residue field gives p^11=p^-1; a direct check of all twelve nonzero residues agrees. Thus the shift from exponent 11 to -1 is meaningful and both powers are plainly present in the ink. S047-UNIT: Given (3.7) and c(13)≡12 modulo 13, induction makes each c(13^alpha) a unit modulo 13, justifying the normalization in its corresponding residue ring. S047-RAMIFIED: Divide (3.7) by c(13^alpha); its n=1 instance identifies the scalar with t(13), yielding (3.10). These deductions use (3.7) as an input, rather than independently establishing it.

S047-ZERO-POWER: The second-order recurrence modulo 13 has companion matrix [[t(p),-p^-1],[1,0]], which is invertible. Set a_-1=0 and a_0=1. Some positive power of that matrix is the identity in the finite group GL_2(F_13); at that return a_(h-1)=0. Since the matrix is not the identity, h≥2, so theta=h-1 is positive. This verifies the local recurrence argument under (3.2). The stronger (3.11) is considered with its definition of P on scan48.
